summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web tool that tells you whether a spot near the Moon’s south pole is a good place to land, why, and when. You pick a landing date and select any point on a map of the south pole. The tool answers in plain words: suitable or not, which limits pass or fail (sunlight at landing, a direct view of Earth, the longest dark stretch, the share of the mission with Earth in view), and which landing dates in the next 60 days would work. It can also search the whole region south of 85°S for the best sites on a given date. Existing tools give this information one site and one moment at a time, in interfaces built for specialists. Ours puts Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons together with LOLA terrain and turns them into a decision a mission planner, a teacher or a curious member of the public can read in seconds. That matters because small changes in place or date near the pole change power and communication a great deal, and schedules slip.
details:
What it does

  • Shows a map of the lunar south pole lit as it will be at any hour from 15 November 2026 to 15 November 2027. Shadows are cast from real terrain. A Play button moves them through time.
  • Gives a verdict for any point you select: suitable or not for your landing date and mission length, with each reason shown as a yes or no and the number behind it.
  • Lists the landing dates that work at that site, grouped into runs, so you can see how much room the schedule has to slip.
  • Searches the region south of 85°S for the best sites on a chosen date and shades them on the map.
  • Compares several sites across a range of landing dates in a grid and a sortable table, with hard constraints, slip tolerance (how many days earlier or later a landing can move before a constraint fails), and a mark for candidates that no other candidate beats on every measure.
  • Offers three views of the same model: Mission planner (every input and the full scorecard), Educator (explanations and three solar panel types side by side) and Explorer (a plain-language account for the public).

How it works

The model has five layers, each using only the one below it.

  1. Geometry. The elevation and compass direction of the Sun and Earth at a site come from the points on the Moon directly beneath them (from JPL Horizons) and a dot-product formula. Earth’s position is corrected from the Moon’s centre to the site.
  2. Horizon. A terrain skyline is built for each site from every elevation-map cell within 200 km, in 1° compass bins, with an exact spherical formula for the angle of each cell.
  3. Events. The tool finds when the Sun and Earth cross the skyline, giving rises, sets, visibility windows and time remaining.
  4. Metrics. It reports the share of the mission each body is visible, the longest gaps, and equivalent full-sun hours for three panel types: flat, upright Sun-following and upright fixed.
  5. Decision. Hard constraints filter candidates, and the tool reports slip tolerance and comparisons across sites and dates.

What we verified

  • Sun and Earth elevation and direction agree with JPL Horizons to within 0.003° at the Apollo 11 site and at a site 0.55° from the south pole.
  • The terrain skyline passes synthetic test cases with known answers: a smooth sphere, an observer 1 km above it, a site below the reference height, and a lone peak.
  • The floor of Shackleton crater, a known permanently shadowed region, comes out dark on every day of the year.
  • At an equatorial site the tool finds about 14.8 days of light followed by 14.8 days of dark, as expected.

Limits we state openly

  • Rise and set times against terrain are not yet checked against an independent reference. Our next step is to compare them with NASA’s two-hourly south-pole illumination visualisations.
  • Visibility uses the centre of the Sun’s and Earth’s disks.
  • The 240 m map misses boulders and small ridges. The map view and the site search use coarser grids and are guides; the verdict uses the finer skyline.
  • We do not model landing safety, temperature, ground stations, link budgets or battery sizing. “Suitable” means the site passes the chosen sunlight and Earth-visibility limits.

Benefits and goals

A planner whose launch slips can see in one screen whether the site still works and for how long. An educator can show why a ridge and a crater floor 13 km apart are completely different places to land. Our goal was a tool whose every number can be traced to NASA data and a formula we checked.

Tools and languages

JavaScript, HTML canvas and SVG for the tool, which runs entirely in the browser as one file with no server. Python with NumPy and Pillow to prepare the terrain data. Node.js for the tests. Git, GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting.

NASA Data

  • JPL Horizons System. Hourly sub-solar point, sub-Earth point and Earth–Moon distance for one year, in the Moon’s mean-Earth frame. These drive every Sun and Earth position in the tool. We also used Horizons, run for sites on the lunar surface, as the independent reference for checking our geometry.
  • Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA). The polar gridded elevation product LDEM_60S_240M, at 240 m per pixel. We cropped it to 78°S for site skylines and averaged it to 480 m for the built-in map.
  • “A New View of the Lunar South Pole from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter” (Barker et al., NASA Technical Reports Server). Used to confirm the LOLA products, their pixel scales and their reference frame.
  • NASA Scientific Visualization Studio, “Illumination at the Moon’s South Pole to 80°S, 2025 to 2028”. Identified as the reference for checking our sunlight results. That check is planned and not yet done.
  • QuickMap and Moon Trek. Used to explore the south-pole terrain and to understand the gap the challenge describes.

Use of AI

We used AI tools, as follows.

  • Claude (Anthropic) worked with us as a co-designer of the mathematical model and wrote the code for the tool, the data preparation and the tests, under our direction. We set the scope, made the design decisions recorded in our model specification, ran the JPL Horizons queries, sourced the LOLA data, and reviewed the results. The repository README and the page footer state that the code was written with AI assistance.
  • Google NotebookLM, Chatgpt reviewed the model specification for errors. We checked each finding before adopting or rejecting it.
  • No AI-generated images, video or audio are used. The map is computed from NASA LOLA elevation data and JPL Horizons positions.
